chapter: Chapter 10: Raising Money in a Bubble
section: Do you need to raise at all?
content:
Here is the question my own history forces into this chapter. And it's not rhetorical.  
I never raised because I never needed to. The products paid for themselves. The costs stayed small. And every time I ran the thought experiment (*what, specifically, would an investor's money buy that revenue can't?*), I couldn't produce an answer crisp enough to justify selling a piece of the company and strapping myself to the treadmill above.  
That's not a boast, and it's not a philosophy. It's a test. I want to hand it to you, because the loudest year in venture history is precisely when nobody remembers to administer it.

chapter: Chapter 10: Raising Money in a Bubble
section: The test
content:
Write down the specific things a round would buy: engineers, compute, a sales team, 18 months of your own salary. Then ask, for each one: could customers buy it instead, just slower?  
If the honest answer is "yes, slower," then what you're really buying with venture money is **speed**. And speed is only worth its price in markets where arriving second means arriving dead.  
Some AI markets are like that:  
- When there's a genuine land grab.
- When network effects or data flywheels (Chapter 4) reward whoever gets big first.
- When your costs are front-loaded in compute you can't defer.  
Many are not. A vertical AI product for dental practices does not have winner-take-all dynamics. It has "who built the thing dentists actually trust" dynamics. And trust compounds at the same speed regardless of your cap table.

chapter: Chapter 10: Raising Money in a Bubble
section: The math quietly changed
content:
Here's the part of the bootstrap case that's new, not nostalgic. This book's earlier chapters quietly rewrote the math.  
The classic reason to raise was that building software required a *team* before it required *revenue*. Salaries first, customers later, capital to bridge the gap.  
Chapter 6 showed that gap collapsing. One founder with AI tools now ships what used to take five engineers. The bridge venture capital existed to finance is, for many products, just *shorter* now.  
AI didn't only create the most fundable startup category in history. It also created the cheapest era ever to *not* fundraise in. Almost no one in 2025's gold rush noticed the second fact, because the people who fund the ecosystem have no reason to advertise it.

chapter: Chapter 10: Raising Money in a Bubble
section: The option you keep is worth more than it looks
content:
A bootstrapped company can:  
- Pivot without permission.
- Run profitably at a size no fund would tolerate.
- Sell early for a number that changes your life but wouldn't return a venture fund.
- Simply keep going through a winter, because nobody's term sheet expires.  
Every one of those doors closes, or at least sticks, the day you take institutional money. Not because investors are villains. Because you've contractually agreed to want what they want: the big outcome on the schedule.

chapter: Chapter 10: Raising Money in a Bubble
section: Now the honesty in the other direction
content:
Bootstrapping has its own mythology, and I refuse to trade one romance for another.  
Bootstrapping is not morally superior. It's an instrument with its own failure modes. If your product genuinely needs capital ahead of revenue (heavy compute, a real land grab, regulated markets with long sales cycles), then refusing to raise isn't discipline. It's a decision to lose slowly while better-funded competitors define the category.  
And self-funding has a quieter cost this book takes seriously. When the company eats your savings instead of a fund's, the stress lands on your kitchen table, not a portfolio.  
> 💡 **In one line:** Raising is a choice with a price, not a milestone with a trophy.  
In a year when two-thirds of venture capital is sprinting toward your category, the founder who can articulate exactly why they're taking the money, or exactly why they're not, is rarer than either kind of company.

chapter: Chapter 10: Raising Money in a Bubble
section: The playbook: how a raise actually happens
content:
Suppose you've run the test and the answer is yes. The money buys something revenue can't, and the speed is worth the price. Now what? Who do you even email?  
This is the part every fundraising chapter written by insiders skips, because to them it's as obvious as breathing. I've never run this play myself, so I'll do what I did all book: assemble it from the people who have and who wrote it down honestly.  
Two sources anchor this section.  
- **Y Combinator's seed-fundraising guide**, the closest thing the process has to official documentation.
- **Ankur Warikoo**, the founder of nearbuy, who raised over **$40 million** from Sequoia and Paytm, ran the company for years, exited, and now tells Indian founders the things he wishes someone had told him.  
I lean on Warikoo deliberately. He's seen the machine from inside, he has nothing left to sell you about it, and his framing is the clearest one-sentence take I've found:  
> *"Investors are not in the business of supporting startups. They're in the business of entering and exiting businesses."*  
Hold that sentence through everything that follows. It isn't cynicism. It's the user manual.

chapter: Chapter 10: Raising Money in a Bubble
section: Step one: match the money to the need
content:
Money comes in escalating tiers, and each tier buys a different relationship:  
1. Your own savings.
2. Friends and family.
3. Angel investors (individuals writing personal checks).
4. Seed funds.
5. Only then, the institutional venture firms.  
Warikoo's advice to founders who don't need huge capital: start at the smallest tier that works. Friends, family, colleagues, people betting on *you*, before institutions betting on an *exit*.  
The corporate version is "raise from the right stage of investor." It's why emailing a growth fund about your pre-revenue idea isn't ambition, it's a sorting error.  
Decide the amount the same way. Take the milestone from earlier in this chapter, cost it month by month, add real buffer, and that's the raise. Not "as much as possible." The amount defines the dilution, the valuation expectation, and the size of the promise you're making.

chapter: Chapter 10: Raising Money in a Bubble
section: Step two: build the list before you send anything
content:
A raise is a sales process. Like any sales process, it starts with a qualified pipeline, not inspiration.  
Aim for **30 to 50 names**: investors who actually write checks at your stage, in your domain, who haven't funded your direct competitor. Their portfolios are public. An hour with their websites tells you who belongs on the list.  
Then rank it. And here's the unintuitive move: **practice on the bottom tier first.** Your pitch will be measurably better by meeting ten than it was at meeting one. You want your dream investors to get the version that's been sharpened on people whose "no" costs you nothing.

chapter: Chapter 10: Raising Money in a Bubble
section: Step three: get introduced, or earn the cold email
content:
The currency of access is the warm intro. And the best source isn't a banker or a mutual friend. It's founders the investor has already backed.  
A portfolio founder saying "you should meet this person" is pre-validation. It tells the investor that someone they trusted with money trusts you with their name.  
No network yet? Build one honestly. The venture cliché worth keeping is Mark Suster's **"invest in lines, not dots."** Investors fund trajectories they've watched, not snapshots they've just met.  
- Start months before you raise.
- Send short, specific progress updates to investors you'd want someday.
- By the time you formally pitch, you're not a stranger with a deck. You're a line they've been watching go up.  
And if cold is all you have, cold works better than folklore claims. Provided the email is five sentences, leads with traction, and reads like it could only have been written to that one investor.

chapter: Chapter 10: Raising Money in a Bubble
section: Step four: run it hot, in parallel, on a clock
content:
The single biggest first-timer error is raising *sequentially*. One investor at a time, waiting weeks for each verdict. That hands every investor a free option on you, and produces the slow drip that reads, to the market, as staleness.  
The YC doctrine is the opposite: **compress everything.**  
- Batch your meetings into a tight window.
- Talk to everyone at once.
- Let them know, politely and without bluffing, that others are looking.  
Investor decisions are driven by scarcity and momentum more than analysis. The only honest lever you have on price and speed is simultaneous interest.  
This is also a full-time job. Plan for the raise to consume the CEO entirely for two or three months, and arrange the company so it keeps shipping without you. Nothing kills a round like traction flatlining *during* it.

chapter: Chapter 10: Raising Money in a Bubble
section: Step five: it's not done until the money is in the bank
content:
A verbal yes is not a yes. A term sheet is not money.  
Founders have celebrated at every stage of that sequence, then watched deals die in diligence or vanish when the market hiccuped. Keep every conversation warm until the wire clears. And then, only then, stop fundraising and go back to work.  
Braided through all five steps is Warikoo's larger warning, the one that connects this playbook back to everything before it:  
> *"You can't speed up progress beyond what is sustainable."*  
The process above will get you the meeting, maybe the money. Whether the money builds your company or builds your trap depends on everything that came before this section: the milestone, the valuation, the honest answer about whether you needed it at all.

chapter: Chapter 10: Raising Money in a Bubble
section: What happens in the room
content:
If you do raise, here's the part I can reconstruct from the public record and from every founder postmortem worth reading.  
The meeting itself is mostly four questions wearing different costumes. And you've already done the work for all of them if you've read this far.  
**"What's your moat?"** is Chapter 4. The wrong answer is "our proprietary AI." The right answer names something that compounds and that a model release can't delete: your data flywheel, your workflow lock-in, your distribution, your accumulated trust in a vertical the labs will never specialize in.  
**"What happens when OpenAI ships this?"** is Chapter 5. In 2025-era diligence it stopped being a gotcha and became a standard checklist item. The founders who fumble it answer "we hope they don't." The founders who nail it show that their value lives in the part of the stack the labs structurally won't build. They can say "the model is rented; here's what we own" without rehearsing.  
**"What are your unit economics?"** is Chapter 9, now asked at stages where it never used to come up, because every investor has watched the Stability AI movie. Know your cost per customer, your margin trajectory, and what happens to both when usage doubles. "We'll figure out pricing later" reads, in this market, as "we are the GPU bill's next victim."  
**"Why is your AI real?"** is the newest one. It's asked *because* of Builder.ai and Nate, not despite them. Expect technical diligence on what your product actually does versus what the deck implies. The preparation is simple and most founders still skip it: make the deck say exactly what's true. Then diligence becomes a demo instead of an interrogation.

chapter: Chapter 10: Raising Money in a Bubble
section: Remember: you're choosing them too
content:
There's a question first-time founders almost never ask back. It's the one the whole power dynamic is designed to make you forget.  
> 💡 **In one line:** You are also choosing them.  
An investor is a co-owner you can't fire, attached to you for a decade. Longer than most marriages that end.  
> ✅ **Do this:** Ask what happens to their support when a company misses a milestone. Ask for the names of founders from their portfolio whose companies *failed*, and call those founders.  
How an investor behaves in a portfolio company's worst year is the only fact about them that matters. And it's the one fact the pitch process is structured never to reveal.  
In a frothy market, capital is abundant and judgment is scarce. Which means, strange as it sounds, you can afford to be picky precisely when everyone else is sprinting to say yes.

chapter: Chapter 10: Raising Money in a Bubble
section: How to raise sane in a frothy market
content:
So, concretely, if you do raise: how do you fundraise without getting high on your own multiple? A handful of principles. All of them are just this book's spine applied to the cap table.  
**Raise for a milestone, not for a mood.** Know the specific, fundable thing your next round needs to see, and raise exactly enough to reach it with margin. "We raised because we could" is how you over-promise on valuation.  
**Build the durable thing the bubble is distracting everyone from.** When capital is easy, discipline is rare, and discipline becomes the edge. The companies that walked out of the dotcom crash alive had real revenue and real retention while their peers had traffic and a story. Be the boring one with revenue.  
**Make your AI story true and your moat story honest.** You'll be asked "what's your moat?" and "what if a lab does this?" Chapters 3, 4, and 5 are your answers. A founder who can say *"the model is rented, here's what we own"* is far more fundable, in a sober room, than one selling a thin wrapper at a thick multiple.  
**Watch your own unit economics, because investors now do.** The era of funding pure growth with no path to margin is cooling. The AI companies raising well increasingly show they make money per customer, not lose it. Even the headline counterexample proves the rule: Cursor's eye-watering valuation came *after* its revenue ran from $100 million to $2 billion in run-rate. The price was keeping pace with money actually arriving. Chapter 9 isn't just an operations chapter; it's a fundraising chapter now.  
**Treat every dollar as runway through a possible winter.** Plan for the correction you can't time. The founders who survive downturns are the ones who, in the good times, kept enough cash and enough discipline to still be standing when the easy money left. And easy money always, eventually, leaves.

chapter: Chapter 10: Raising Money in a Bubble
section: You're not raising from the bubble. You're surviving it.
content:
Here's the reframe to carry out of this chapter.  
The bubble is not your opportunity. It's your **weather**. You can't control whether it's sunny or about to storm, and trying to time it precisely is a fool's errand even for professionals. What you control is the boat.  
A real business sails through both the boom and the bust:  
- Solving a real problem.
- Owning something the model doesn't.
- Making money on each customer.
- Holding enough runway to outlast a cold season.  
A hype-funded shell with a beautiful valuation and no fundamentals sails through exactly one of them.  
If the money makes sense, raise it. Smart capital at honest terms is a real tool, and this market offers it in historic quantities. If it doesn't, the era has never been kinder to the founder who declines.  
> 🧾 **Receipt:** I'm living proof that the door marked "no thanks" leads somewhere real.  
Just never confuse the valuation for the achievement. The valuation is a number someone assigned to a future you haven't built yet. The achievement is building it.  
In a year when AI startups raised two-thirds of all venture capital, and a chorus of the world's most serious investors warned that much of it would evaporate, the founders who'll still be here in five years are the ones who kept their heads either way. The ones who heard "you're worth a fortune" and quietly answered: *not yet, but we're going to be.*

chapter: Chapter 10: Raising Money in a Bubble
section: Raising money in a bubble, in a nutshell
content:
> 💡 **In one line:** A high valuation isn't a prize you won, it's a milestone you now have about 18 months to justify, so raise for a real reason or don't raise at all.  
**The big ideas:**  
- **It's a bubble *and* it's real.** AI took ~65% of 2025 US venture dollars (up from ~47%), capital loops in circles (Nvidia's $100B to OpenAI, OpenAI's $300B Oracle deal, AMD's $34B warrants), yet OpenAI (~$20B) and Anthropic (~$30B) have real, fast-growing revenue. Like dotcom: Pets.com died, Amazon survived a ~90% fall.
- **A bust financed by cash, not debt, is less systemic.** A correction here looks like 2000, not 2008. Survivable, if you have runway.
- **Don't brand as AI. *Be* AI where it's true.** The label brings ~38% higher Series A valuations (up to ~193% at later stages), but AI-washing gets punished: Presto, Nate, Builder.ai (raised ~$445M, went bankrupt).
- **A high valuation is a debt, not a trophy.** It's a milestone with a clock. Miss it and you face a down round: re-priced options, anti-dilution transfers, a public signal of trouble.
- **The trap is widest in a froth.** Valuations inflate fastest exactly when the market is most likely to cool, leaving you stranded above your own next round.
- **You may not need to raise at all.** AI made building cheaper (Chapter 6). If customers could buy it, just slower, you're only buying speed, which is only worth it in a true land grab.
- **Raise sane:** raise for a milestone not a mood, build durable revenue, keep your AI and moat stories honest, watch your unit economics, and treat every dollar as runway through a possible winter.  
> ✅ **Do this:** Before you raise, write down exactly what the money buys and ask whether customers could fund it instead. If they could (just slower), and arriving second doesn't kill you, build it with revenue. If you do raise, size it to a specific milestone with two-plus years of runway, and never confuse the valuation for the achievement.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: Opening
content:
*> The law protects human minds. AI output becomes yours only by passing through one.*  
> ⚖️ **Not legal advice:** I'm a founder, not a lawyer, and nothing here is legal advice. This chapter is here to help you spot the landmines early, so you know when to call a real lawyer. It is not a substitute for one. For anything specific to your company, get a real lawyer. I mean it more in this chapter than in any other.  
In September 2025, Anthropic agreed to pay authors **$1.5 billion**. That is the largest copyright settlement in American history. It worked out to roughly **$3,000 per book**, for about **half a million books** the company had downloaded from pirate libraries to train its models. Anthropic makes Claude. It is one of the two or three most important AI companies on earth.  
Now read this. Three months *earlier*, in the very same case, a federal judge had ruled that training an AI on books was fair use. Legal. As long as the books were lawfully acquired.  
Read those two facts again. Same company. Same models. Same year. The training was legal. The downloading cost a billion and a half.  
That is the current state of AI law in one anecdote. Not lawless. *Jagged.* Full of distinctions sharp enough to cut a company in half.  
> **Key term: copyright.** The legal right to control who copies, sells, or reuses an original work (text, art, code, music). It belongs to the creator by default.  
> **Key term: fair use.** A US legal defense that lets you copy a protected work without permission in some cases (commentary, research, transformation). Decided case by case, never guaranteed.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: Opening
content:
> **Key term: fair use.** A US legal defense that lets you copy a protected work without permission in some cases (commentary, research, transformation). Decided case by case, never guaranteed.  
> 🧾 **Receipt:** Here is my own confession. Until I researched this chapter, I hadn't seriously thought about half of these questions for my own products. And I've been shipping AI features for years. My apps have generated images using other people's models. They've generated subtitles and content that customers paid for. One of them holds live operational data for other people's companies. Do I own those outputs? Could my users' data end up somewhere I never intended? I'd never asked.  
If you're wincing in recognition, this chapter is for you. We can wince together.  
The point is not to make either of us a lawyer. It's to make us aware of the landmines early enough to know when to *call* one. The founder who learns these issues exist after they've bitten is the one who pays the most to fix them.  
Four questions, in order of how badly founders underestimate them.  
1. Do you own what the AI made?
2. Who's liable when AI-made things break?
3. What is your team already leaking?
4. Does a European law you've never read apply to little you?

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: Do You Own What the AI Made?
content:
Start with the most counterintuitive landmine. Nearly every founder assumes the opposite.  
You may not legally own the things your AI generated for you.  
> ⚠️ **Myth:** "If my AI made it, I own it." Often false. A purely AI-made logo, line of copy, or block of code may belong to no one at all.  
The cleanest way to see this is through two real cases. One is absolutist. One is painfully practical.

> ⚠️ **Myth:** "If my AI made it, I own it." Often false. A purely AI-made logo, line of copy, or block of code may belong to no one at all.  
The cleanest way to see this is through two real cases. One is absolutist. One is painfully practical.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: The absolutist case: a machine can't be an author
content:
The absolutist case is *Thaler v. Perlmutter*. Stephen Thaler is a computer scientist. He built an AI system he calls the Creativity Machine. In 2018 he tried to register a copyright for an image it produced, called "A Recent Entrance to Paradise." He listed the *machine* as the author.  
The Copyright Office refused. Thaler sued, and kept suing, all the way up.  
In March 2025, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the refusal. Under US law, an author is a human being. Full stop. In March 2026, the Supreme Court declined to hear the case. That makes the principle about as settled as law gets: **a machine cannot be an author, and a work with no human author has no copyright at all.**  
Not "weak copyright." None. It belongs to no one.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: The practical case: a prompt isn't authorship
content:
Thaler was a deliberate test case. He *wanted* the machine listed as author. The case that should actually keep you up at night is the practical one: *Zarya of the Dawn*.  
Kris Kashtanova, a New York artist, made a comic book. She wrote the story, designed the characters, composed the pages. And she generated the artwork with Midjourney.  
In February 2023, the Copyright Office split the baby with surgical precision:  
- The **text**? Kashtanova's. Protected.
- The **selection, coordination, and arrangement** of images and words into a book? Kashtanova's. Protected.
- The individual Midjourney **images themselves**? Not protected. Not Kashtanova's. Not anybody's.  
The Office's reasoning is the part worth memorizing. A person who writes a prompt doesn't actually *form* the image that comes back. Midjourney starts from visual noise, and the prompt merely *influences* the outcome.  
Think of a photographer. They control framing, lighting, exposure, subject. A prompter just makes a request and accepts what arrives. Influence is not authorship.  
The Copyright Office's **2025 report** on AI and copyrightability confirmed this as standing policy. Prompts alone, however refined, do not make you the author of what the machine produces.  
> 💡 **In one line:** A prompt is a request, not an act of authorship.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: Run your own company through the Zarya split
content:
Now run your own company through the *Zarya* split. It maps one-to-one.  
- The logo your AI generated while you typed adjectives at it? That's a Midjourney image. Likely un-ownable. Which means, in principle, a competitor who copies it outright may be infringing nothing.
- The product description your AI wrote and you shipped word-for-word? Same exposure.
- But your app's interface, where you selected, arranged, edited, and integrated a hundred AI outputs into one designed whole? That arrangement is *yours*. The way Kashtanova's book, as a book, is hers.  
The legal line runs exactly along the line of your involvement.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: Relief: the logo still has a backup protection
content:
Before you panic about the logo, one piece of genuine relief. Copyright is not the only protection a logo has.  
> **Key term: trademark.** Legal protection for a mark (a name, a logo) that identifies your business in commerce. It doesn't care who or what *drew* the mark. It cares that customers associate it with *you*.  
So the AI-generated logo you can't copyright can still be registered and defended as a trademark, once you're actually using it as your brand. [Lawyer-check, qualitative.]  
The exposure is real but narrower than it first sounds. A competitor reproducing your un-copyrighted marketing *images* may be untouchable. A competitor slapping your *logo* on their product is still infringing your trademark.  
The general principle holds: the cheapest insurance is still putting a human hand visibly into anything you'd sue over.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: Two follow-ups: code and patents
content:
Two questions arrive immediately. Let's take them.  
**What about code?** Same logic, same line. The Copyright Office's framework doesn't carve out an exception for software. Code generated entirely by a model from a prompt sits in the same un-ownable territory as the Midjourney images. Code a human meaningfully wrote, modified, structured, and assembled is protectable like any other human work.  
For most real codebases, AI drafts and humans architect, review, and rework. The practical product is a thoroughly human-authored work with AI assistance. That's also roughly how you should describe it if an acquirer's lawyers ever ask.  
**What about patents?** The same Stephen Thaler spent years trying to have his AI system named as an *inventor* on patent applications around the world. Patent offices and courts have overwhelmingly said no. An inventor, like an author, must be human.  
The pattern across both regimes is identical. Here's the sentence to remember: **the law protects human minds, and AI output becomes yours by passing through one.**

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: The fix is cheap
content:
That suggests the fix, and it's cheap.  
1. **Put human judgment into the assets you need to own.** Choose among many generations. Modify. Combine. Refine. The more you genuinely shape the output, the more ownable it becomes.
2. **Document it.** Keep the drafts, the iterations, the records of what a human changed. If ownership is ever contested, the file showing fifty edits is the difference between "AI-generated" and "AI-assisted, human-authored."
3. **Notice your moat.** This quietly reinforces Chapter 4: a pile of purely AI-generated assets was never going to be your moat anyway. Anyone's AI can generate the same pile. What the law protects, and what competition respects, turn out to be the same thing: what *you* did with it.  
> ✅ **Do this:** For anything you'd want to defend in court, keep the edit history. Drafts and iterations turn "AI-generated" into "AI-assisted, human-authored."

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: When the AI's Code Breaks, Who's Liable?
content:
The short, unwelcome answer: you are.  
> **Key term: liability.** Legal responsibility for harm or loss. If you're "liable," you're the one who pays.  
Whatever ships under your company's name is your responsibility. A senior engineer wrote it, an intern wrote it, or a model wrote it at 2 a.m. It doesn't matter. The law treats your product as *your* product. "The AI wrote that part" is not a defense. No more than "my employee wrote that part" would be.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: The Air Canada precedent
content:
You met this principle in Chapter 1. A Canadian tribunal ordered Air Canada to honor a bereavement-fare refund policy that its support chatbot had invented out of thin air.  
The airline's defense deserves to be quoted at parties. It argued that the chatbot was "a separate legal entity responsible for its own actions."  
The tribunal did not dignify that for long. Negligent misrepresentation. Company liable. Pay the man.  
The damages were **812 Canadian dollars**. The precedent was priceless. A company is responsible for what its AI tells customers, in the same confident tone it says everything. The bot's hallucination was the company's debt.  
Yours will be too. And yours is unlikely to cost $812.  
> 💡 **In one line:** You own your product's output the way you own an employee's. The AI is not a co-defendant.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: Three practical consequences
content:
These are cheaper to absorb now than later.  
1. **Your own terms of service are your turn to play vendor.** The same risk-shifting clauses you're about to resent in OpenAI's terms (disclaimers, accuracy warnings, liability caps) belong in *your* contracts with *your* customers. Drafted by someone who does this for a living. Risk in this industry flows downhill until a contract stops it. Make sure yours isn't the open valve.
2. **Human review is a legal control, not just a quality one.** Everywhere your AI's output carries real consequences (advice, money, anything customer-binding), a documented human checkpoint is the difference between "negligence" and "a reviewed process that failed." Those price very differently in court.
3. **Insurance has caught up. Make sure yours has.** Technology errors-and-omissions policies increasingly ask about AI use. A policy bought before you shipped AI features may not contemplate them. That's a renewal-time conversation that costs an hour and can save the company. [Lawyer/broker-check: practice advice, not sourced doctrine.]

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: The other side of the deal: read your vendor's terms
content:
Now read the other side of the deal you've signed with your model vendor. They have thought about this far more carefully than you have.  
The standard AI-vendor terms (OpenAI's are representative) do three things:  
- Disclaim warranties. Output is provided "as is."
- Instruct you to evaluate output for accuracy before relying on it.
- Cap the vendor's total liability at something tidy. Commonly, your last **twelve months of fees**.  
Sit with that asymmetry for a second. If your AI feature destroys a customer's business, your exposure is whatever a court says it is. Your vendor's exposure, to you, is a refund.  
The model provider has contractually arranged for nearly all the risk to flow downhill. And downhill is where you live.  
  
There is, as of this writing, no landmark verdict cleanly dividing blame when AI-written code fails in production. The area is genuinely unsettled. [Lawyer-check.] In practice, assume the buck stops at whoever shipped to the customer.  
Build, test, and insure accordingly. And triple it anywhere your product touches money, health, safety, or the law. Which is also exactly where the EU's regulators, later in this chapter, will be waiting.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: The Fine Print That Protects You (Sometimes)
content:
Here's the twist most founders don't know. The big vendors *will* stand behind you on one specific risk: copyright claims over model output. But only if you're paying them properly. And only if you read the conditions.  
> **Key term: indemnification.** A promise by one party to cover another's legal costs and damages if a specific kind of lawsuit hits. Here: the vendor agrees to defend you if their AI's output gets you sued for copyright.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: The shields, and their shape
content:
Microsoft moved first, with its **Customer Copyright Commitment**. If a third party sues you claiming Copilot's output infringes their copyright, Microsoft will defend you and pay the judgment. *Provided* you used the product with its guardrails and content filters turned on. Turn the filters off, and the shield evaporates.  
OpenAI followed with **Copyright Shield**: indemnification for output-based copyright claims. But only for ChatGPT Enterprise and the API.  
Google offers a two-pronged version, covering both its training data and its generated output, for paying cloud customers.  
Notice the pattern in all of them:  
- The protection covers **paying business tiers**. Not free or consumer accounts.
- It typically **excludes** output you got by fine-tuning on your own data, or by deliberately prompting for someone's protected work.
- It requires you to have **used the safety features**.  
The shields are real. But they're shaped like the vendors' interests. They protect the customers who pay and behave.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: Turn the fine print into a checklist
content:
This turns the fine print into a checklist you can actually use. When you sign with any AI vendor (model provider, AI-powered SaaS, anything), four clauses tell you most of what matters:  
1. **Training rights.** May they train on your data? Is the answer different on your tier?
2. **Retention.** How long do they keep what you send?
3. **Indemnification.** If their output gets you sued, do they defend you, and under what conditions?
4. **Liability cap.** When their product fails you, what's their maximum exposure? Is it twelve months of fees against your company's existence?  
  
> ✅ **Do this:** Ten minutes with those four answers, before you sign, is the cheapest legal work you will ever do.  
---

section: The Training-Data Wars (and Why Provenance Suddenly Matters)
content:
There's a second IP front, further from your desk but shaping every tool on it: the lawsuits over what the models were *trained* on.  
> **Key term: training data.** The huge pile of text, images, and code a model learns from. The fights below are over whether the labs had the right to use it.  
Authors, news organizations, and developers have sued the labs for ingesting their work without permission. Starting in 2025, the courts began to answer. The answers split. And the split is the lesson.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: Three rulings, three outcomes
content:
**February 2025: *Thomson Reuters v. Ross*.** A judge rejected the fair-use defense outright. Ross had trained a legal-research AI on Westlaw's headnotes to build a product that *competed with Westlaw*. That, the court said, is not fair use.  
**Four months later: *Bartz v. Anthropic*.** Judge Alsup ruled that training a language model on lawfully purchased books *is* fair use. "Quintessentially transformative." But Anthropic's separate stash of half a million **pirated** books was plain infringement. That's the ruling that matured into the **$1.5 billion** settlement this chapter opened with.  
**The same month: *Kadrey v. Meta*.** Judge Chhabria sided with Meta on the record before him, while pointedly leaving the door open. A plaintiff who could *show* that AI training floods the market and devalues authors' work might well win on a future record.  
And the biggest one, **The New York Times v. OpenAI**, grinds on. In January 2026, a court compelled OpenAI to hand over **twenty million ChatGPT conversation logs** in discovery. A reminder that what your users type into an AI product can end up as evidence in someone else's lawsuit.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: Closer to your stack: the Copilot suit
content:
Closer to your stack: the **GitHub Copilot class action**. Developers alleged that Copilot reproduced their open-source code without the required attribution. It has been mostly gutted. Narrowed from a sweeping copyright reckoning down to surviving contract and license theories.  
But the underlying mechanism it complained about is real, and it's yours to manage. A code model can reproduce licensed snippets without their licenses attached. A fragment of GPL-licensed code pasted by a model into your proprietary codebase is a contamination question. You'd rather answer it in code review than in diligence for your acquisition.  
(A once-popular statistic claiming ~35 percent of AI code samples carry licensing irregularities turns out to trace to nothing solid, so I won't use it. But the qualitative risk is documented, and the discipline is the same: scan, attribute, and know your dependencies.)

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: Why Ross lost where the others won
content:
Read the difference. It's the part that applies to *you*.  
Ross trained on Westlaw's content to build a *substitute* for Westlaw. The training data and the target market were the same. Fair use has never smiled on copying your competitor to compete with them.  
The book cases were "transformative." Novels in, general-purpose language model out. No substitute for the novels.  
Now apply that lens to your own roadmap. If your plan involves fine-tuning a model on scraped content from the very industry player you intend to displace (their listings, their reviews, their documentation), you are running the *Ross* pattern, not the *Anthropic* one. And 2025's case law suggests the courts will notice.  
Scraping "public" data was a gray-area growth hack for two decades. It is rapidly becoming a provenance liability with named precedents. If your data strategy can't survive the question "whose work is this, and are we competing with them?", fix the strategy before someone else's lawyer asks.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: Samsung: the famous casualty
content:
In the spring of 2023, engineers at Samsung leaked. A company whose security culture guards some of the most valuable industrial secrets on earth.  
They reportedly did three things:  
- Pasted proprietary semiconductor source code into ChatGPT to debug it.
- Fed in test sequences to optimize them.
- Uploaded the transcript of an internal meeting to have the AI write minutes.  
Three incidents, roughly twenty days. Each engineer was just saving an hour. Collectively, they had potentially exported crown-jewel IP to an external service whose consumer tier, at the time, used conversations for training.  
Samsung's response: ban generative AI on company devices, and start building internal tools.  
The detail that should stick with you isn't the ban. It's that *nobody involved was malicious.* The leak was made of helpfulness and deadlines. Which your company also runs on.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: The two edges: leakage and regurgitation
content:
Understand the two edges of the danger.  
The first is **leakage**. Where does pasted data go? The answer depends, maddeningly, on which tier of which tool.  
- The **business and API tiers** of the major providers do not train on your data by default. That's the safe lane.
- The **consumer** tiers are the trap. Free and personal ChatGPT use your chats for training unless you opt out.
- And Anthropic, in 2025, *reversed* its consumer policy. Where conversations were previously not used for training, consumer Claude now trains on them unless the user opts out. With **retention of up to five years** for those who opt in.  
I single that one out not to pick on Anthropic, but because it proves the rule that should govern your thinking: **these policies are not stable.** The privacy posture your team relied on last year can be a settings toggle away from gone.  
The second edge is **regurgitation**. Models can memorize fragments of training data and reproduce them for other users on the right prompt. Data that goes in can, in principle, come back out somewhere you don't control. That's how a twenty-minute shortcut becomes a trade-secret problem, a customer-contract breach, or a GDPR incident, depending on what was pasted.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: You are someone's AI-data risk too
content:
If you sell to businesses, this section runs in both directions. Because *you* are someone's AI-data risk.  
The moment your product touches AI, your customers' procurement teams start asking the questions this chapter just taught you to ask:  
- Which model vendors sit behind your product?
- Does anyone train on our data?
- Where is it processed, and for how long?  
Expect the security questionnaire. The data-processing agreement with AI-specific clauses. And, from larger customers, a flat requirement that their data never leave business-tier infrastructure.  
This is not a burden to dodge. It's a sales asset. The founder who can answer "here's our data flow, here's our vendor list, here's what trains on nothing" in one page closes enterprise deals against competitors who answer with a shrug.  
> 🧾 **Receipt:** I learned this from the buyer's side of the table before I ever thought about the legal side. The vendors I trust with my companies' data are the ones who had the answer ready.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: The defenses are within your power
content:
The defenses are unglamorous and entirely within your power.  
1. **Put proprietary data only through business or API tiers.** That one change closes most of the door. It's why Chapter 6's architecture advice routed everything through the API in the first place.
2. **Write a one-page AI-use policy in plain language.** What data may go into which tools. What never goes into any of them (credentials, customer personal data, unreleased financials). And which approved tools make the safe path the *easy* path. Samsung's engineers didn't lack ethics. They lacked a sanctioned tool that did what ChatGPT did.
3. **Set the baseline assumption for everyone, including yourself.** Anything typed into a consumer chatbot may not stay private. That's not paranoia. That's just reading the terms.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: One last mirror: you hold the logs now
content:
One last mirror to look into before we leave data. If you ship an AI product, *you are now the company holding the logs.*  
Remember the New York Times case. A court ordered OpenAI to produce **twenty million** user conversations in discovery. The same mechanism applies at your scale. Everything your users type into your AI feature is a record you hold. And records you hold can be subpoenaed, breached, or demanded by a customer exercising deletion rights you may have promised without checking whether your vendors can honor them.  
So decide on purpose, not by default:  
- What do you log?
- How long do you keep it?
- What do you actually delete when a user clicks delete?
- Do your model vendors' retention policies make a liar of your own privacy page?  
A privacy policy that overpromises is worse than one that's modest and true. Most founders inherit their logging from whatever the framework defaulted to. The ones who chose it deliberately answer a subpoena, a breach, or an enterprise security review without a cold sweat.  
> ✅ **Do this:** Move proprietary work to business or API tiers, and write a one-page AI-use policy. Make the safe path the easy path.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: Does the EU AI Act Apply to You?
content:
Probably more than you'd guess. Because it was built to reach across borders.  
> **Key term: EU AI Act.** The world's first comprehensive AI law, in force since August 2024. It sorts AI systems by risk level and sets duties for each.  
The Act applies not only to European companies, but to anyone whose AI system's output is used by people in the EU. Serve European users, and it can apply to little you, wherever you sit.  
The penalties at the top end are designed to frighten adults: up to **35 million euros or 7 percent of global revenue**, whichever is *higher*.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: Walk the pyramid
content:
Before you panic, walk the structure. The Act is a pyramid, and you're probably near the bottom.  
- **Prohibited practices** (the top). Social scoring, manipulative systems, certain biometric surveillance. Banned outright since February 2025. If these describe your product, you have bigger problems than this chapter.
- **High-risk systems.** AI making consequential decisions about people in hiring, credit, education, medical devices, critical infrastructure. This tier carries the heavy machinery: risk-management systems, data-governance requirements, human oversight, conformity assessments. If your AI screens job candidates or scores loan applications for EU users, budget for real compliance and real counsel.
- **Limited risk.** Where most founder products live. The obligations are mostly *transparency*: tell people when they're talking to a machine rather than a human, and label AI-generated or manipulated content as such.
- **Minimal risk** (the base). Spam filters, inventory forecasting, most boring-AI from Chapter 2. Essentially no new obligations at all.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: Providers vs. deployers
content:
One more distinction the Act makes works in your favor. It separates *providers* from *deployers*.  
> **Key term: providers vs. deployers.** Providers build and supply AI systems and models. Deployers just use them. The heaviest duties land on providers.  
The heaviest general-purpose-model obligations, in force since August 2025, land on the labs whose models you rent. Not on you for renting them. A startup wrapping a frontier model inherits duties appropriate to what it ships, not to what OpenAI ships.  
(Build and train your own substantial model, and you start climbing toward provider territory. One more hidden cost on the "train our own model" path that Chapter 7 already talked you out of.)

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: The founder's two-question test
content:
So the founder's version is a two-question test.  
**Question one:** Does your AI make or shape consequential decisions about individuals (money, jobs, health, education, legal status)? If yes, you're in high-risk territory. Get a lawyer who's read the Act, this quarter.  
**Question two:** If no (your product drafts emails, summarizes documents, generates designs, answers questions), your likely obligations are the disclosure-and-labeling kind. Honest chatbots and labeled AI content. Which you should be doing anyway, because Chapter 8 told you trust is the product.  
One honest caveat: the timeline is still moving. The transparency and high-risk obligations land in stages through August 2026. And Brussels' "Digital Omnibus" package may push parts of the high-risk regime to late 2027.  
Which is itself the meta-lesson of this whole chapter. The rules are being written *while you build*. "I didn't know it applied to me" has never once worked as a defense, in any jurisdiction, for anyone.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: A Founder's Pre-Flight Checklist
content:
Let me compress the chapter into the things to actually *do*. Awareness without action is just anxiety.  
1. **Shape and document the human contribution to anything you need to own.** The *Zarya* line runs along your involvement, so make your involvement deep and provable.
2. **Assume you're liable for everything your product outputs.** Air Canada was. Test the high-stakes paths like the lawsuit depends on it. Because it might.
3. **Before you sign with a vendor, pull the four clauses:** training rights, retention, indemnification and its conditions, liability cap.
4. **Prefer vendors who can explain where their training data came from.** Provenance now has a billion-dollar price tag.
5. **Move every proprietary workflow onto business or API tiers.** Write the one-page AI policy. Give your team a sanctioned tool, so the safe path is the easy one. Remember that Samsung's leak was made of deadlines, not malice.
6. **If you have EU users, run the two-question test.** Know your risk tier before a regulator runs it for you.
7. **The moment any of this stops being general** (a contract, an acquisition, a threat letter, a high-risk classification), stop reading founder books and call an actual lawyer. Early, while it's cheap.  
I'll close where I confessed I started. Most of this chapter is homework I hadn't done for my own companies. The image-generating product whose outputs I assumed I owned. The customer data I'd never traced through a vendor's terms.  
I'm not telling you that to model shame. I'm telling you because the gap between "shipping AI" and "having thought about any of this" is wide enough to hold a multi-product founder who writes books about AI. Which means it's wide enough to hold you.  
None of this is the fun part of building. All of it is the part that, ignored, can quietly undo the company every other chapter taught you to build.

chapter: Chapter 11: Who Owns It, and Who Gets Sued?
section: Legal and IP in a Nutshell
content:
> 💡 **In one line:** The law protects human minds and the people who ship products, so own things by shaping them yourself, assume you're liable for everything your product does, and know where your data came from and where it goes.  
**The big ideas:**  
- **Purely AI-made work may be un-ownable.** A machine can't be an author (*Thaler*), and a prompt isn't authorship (*Zarya*, US Copyright Office 2025). You make output yours by adding real human contribution: selection, arrangement, editing. Document it.
- **You are liable for your product's output.** "The AI wrote it" is not a defense (Air Canada, $812). Vendors disclaim warranties and cap their liability at about twelve months of fees. The risk flows downhill to you.
- **Provenance now has a price tag.** Courts split in 2025: *Thomson Reuters v. Ross* (no fair use), *Bartz v. Anthropic* (lawful books fair use, pirated library infringing, $1.5B settlement), *NYT v. OpenAI* (ongoing, 20 million logs handed over). Know where your data came from.
- **Your team is leaking via shadow AI.** ~38% admit sharing sensitive work info without permission. Business and API tiers generally don't train on your data; consumer ChatGPT and consumer Claude do unless you opt out (retention up to five years).
- **The EU AI Act can reach you anywhere** if you have EU users. Most founder products sit in the lighter transparency tier (label AI content, disclose chatbots). Penalties run to tens of millions of euros or a percent of global revenue. Timeline rolling out 2026–2027, still being amended.  
> ✅ **Do this:** Put a human hand into anything you want to own and keep the edit history. Move proprietary data to business/API tiers. Write the one-page AI policy. Pull the four vendor clauses before you sign. And the moment it gets specific, call a real lawyer, early, while it's cheap.

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: Opening
content:
*> You're not invisible because the machines won't cite you. You're invisible if you have nothing worth citing and no audience of your own.*  
There's a particular dread that arrives the first time you try this. You ask ChatGPT a question your own product answers. It recommends three competitors. It never mentions you.  
It feels like being erased.  
For two decades, "getting found" meant ranking on Google. Now a machine reads the whole web and hands the user a finished answer with a few names in it. If you're not one of those names, you're not in the conversation at all. There isn't even a second page to be on.  
> **Key term: SEO** means Search Engine Optimization: the work of getting your page to show up when people search Google.  
This is the most concrete distribution shift of the AI era. It terrifies founders for good reason. Distribution is the thing that killed two of my own companies, as you read in Chapter 5.  
So let me give you the honest version. The panic is overblown. The hype is a grift. The actual playbook is more reassuring, and more boring, than either.

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: What's Actually Changing
content:
The shift is real and measurable, so let's not soften it.  
Pew Research watched real users browse. They found that when Google shows an AI summary at the top of the page, people click through to an actual website **about half as often**: 8 percent of the time, versus 15 percent without the summary.  
> **Key term: AI Overviews** are the AI-written summaries Google now puts at the top of search results, above the regular blue links.  
It gets worse for the hopeful. Of users who saw an AI summary, only **1 percent** clicked a link inside it. The citation you're fighting for is real. But it's a consolation prize measured in single digits. Mostly, people read the answer and leave. Roughly **26 percent** end the session entirely.  
  
> **Key term: zero-click** means a search that ends without the person clicking through to any website. They got their answer and left.  
And this lands on a web that was already drifting that way. SparkToro found that roughly **60 percent of Google searches already ended without a click** to the open web, before AI summaries became common. AI answers pour accelerant on a fire that was already burning.  
Gartner predicted that traditional search engine **volume** would drop **25 percent by 2026** as questions migrate to chatbots. Read that carefully. It's a prediction, not a measurement. And it's about volume, not traffic. But directionally, nobody serious disputes it.

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: Where the buying decision moved
content:
The clicks are only half the story. The deeper change is *where the buying decision happens.*  
A customer used to search, open five tabs, compare, and decide on your pricing page. Every step was visible in someone's analytics. Every step was a chance to win them.  
Increasingly that whole journey happens inside one conversation. They describe their problem to an assistant. They ask follow-ups. They compare the three names the model offered. They arrive at exactly one website, the winner's, already convinced.  
The funnel didn't shorten. It moved indoors, into a room you can't see.  
That reframes the question this chapter answers. It's no longer "how do I rank?" It's "when the machine summarizes my market to a buyer, am I in the summary, and what does it say?"

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: The sky isn't falling, it's rearranging
content:
Read those numbers right, though. "Search sends fewer clicks" is not "search is dead." If traditional search volume drops a quarter, three-quarters remains. That's still an enormous channel.  
What's actually happening is a **split**. Discovery is fragmenting from one place, the Google results page, into several: the AI summary, the chatbot conversation, the answer engine. Your job is no longer just "rank on Google." It's "be the answer wherever the answer is now given."  
  
> 💡 **In one line:** This is more surface area to win on, not less.  
The sky isn't falling. It's rearranging.

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: GEO Is Mostly Just SEO in a Costume
content:
Into that anxiety has rushed an industry of people selling you "Generative Engine Optimization." GEO. Sometimes AEO, "answer engine optimization." They pitch it as a mysterious new dark art you must pay them to perform.  
> **Key term: GEO** (Generative Engine Optimization) means making your content show up in AI-generated answers, the way SEO meant showing up in Google results.  
Here is the single most money-saving sentence in this chapter: **it is mostly the SEO fundamentals you already knew, pointed at a new reader.**  
> ⚠️ **Myth:** "GEO is a mysterious new dark art you have to buy from a specialist." No. The mystique is invented. The discipline is real, and you mostly already know it.  
Don't take my word for it. Take Google's. Their own developer documentation is blunt: there are no additional technical requirements to appear in AI Overviews beyond the standard eligibility every normal page needs. No secret AI file to add. No special schema. No new markup.  
Their summary sentence deserves framing. Optimizing for generative AI search **"is still SEO."**  
The mechanism makes sense once you remember Chapter 7. These AI answers are largely built *on top of* search. The model retrieves pages and summarizes them. So the things that made you rank, being crawlable, being authoritative, being clearly the best answer to a real question, are the same things that get you *cited*.  
The reader changed. It went from a human skimming blue links to a model deciding what to quote. The fundamentals that earn that citation did not.  
> ✅ **Do this:** When someone offers to sell you a proprietary GEO methodology, hold onto your wallet.  
---

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: What Actually Gets You Cited
content:
That said, the new reader has a few genuine preferences worth knowing. They're not exotic.  
A Princeton-led study tested what actually lifts a page's visibility in AI-generated answers. It's about the only rigorous experiment in this whole hype-soaked category. The winners: adding **citations**, **direct quotations**, and above all **statistics**. Fact-dense, attributable content lifted visibility by **up to 40 percent**.  
The losers: keyword stuffing, the dark art of the old game, did precisely nothing.  
That tells you something true. A model assembling an answer prefers content it can lift cleanly: a clear claim, a real number, a quotable sentence with a source. Vague marketing copy gives it nothing to grab.

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: Show me, don't tell me
content:
Let me make that concrete. "Be quotable and fact-dense" is exactly the kind of advice that nods past people.  
Here's a sentence from the kind of page every startup has:  
*"Our AI-powered platform revolutionizes product imagery for e-commerce sellers, delivering stunning results in seconds."*  
A model can do nothing with that. It's unfalsifiable, unattributable, and interchangeable with ten thousand competitors' homepages.  
Now the same page, rewritten by someone who read this chapter:  
*"Sellers on Amazon India must upload images at 2000×2000 pixels on a pure white background; Flipkart requires 1024×1024. Listings with non-compliant images are rejected automatically. Our tool converts a single phone photo into compliant images for all four major Indian marketplaces in under a minute."*  
That paragraph contains four liftable facts and a specific claim. When someone asks an AI assistant "what are Amazon India's image requirements?", the second version is **citable**, and the citation carries your product with it. (Those requirements are real. I learned them by building exactly that pipeline, mistake by mistake.)  
  
The pattern generalizes. Write the page that answers the question your customer actually asks, with numbers and specifics a machine can quote. You've done most of what GEO consultants charge for.  
> 💡 **In one line:** One page that is genuinely the best answer to one real question beats fifty pages of optimized fog.

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: What other people say beats what you say
content:
The second preference is the one founders underestimate. It ties this chapter back to the whole book: *what other people say about you matters more than what you say about yourself.*  
An analysis of seventy-five thousand brands found that off-site brand **mentions**, being discussed, reviewed, recommended on other sites, on Reddit, on YouTube, correlate with AI visibility far more strongly than backlinks do. Backlinks were the currency of the old game.  
(It's a vendor study, so hold it loosely. But it matches both the Princeton logic and common sense.)  
The model, like a person asking around for a recommendation, trusts the consensus of many voices over your own homepage. So the work isn't only on your site. It's becoming the thing people independently mention: the founder who answers questions in the subreddit where buyers gather, the product named in "what does everyone use for X" threads, the comparison post a happy customer writes unprompted.  
None of that can be faked at scale. Astroturfing communities is detectable, and when detected, fatal to the reputation you're trying to build. The model is, in a sense, just reading the room. Your job is to be well spoken of in the room. Conveniently, that's also just good business.

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: The ten-to-one rule
content:
"Get mentioned in communities" is where most founders either do nothing or do something embarrassing. Here's the discipline that separates reputation from astroturf.  
Find the three or four places your buyers actually talk. For most products that's a couple of subreddits, one professional community, maybe a Discord or a forum old enough to have furniture.  
Then **participate at a ratio of roughly ten to one**: ten genuinely useful contributions for every one time you mention your own product. Answer questions. Share what you've learned. Include the lessons that make you look bad. And when you do mention your product, only do it when it's the honest answer to the question asked, with your affiliation stated plainly.  
This feels excruciatingly slow. That's why almost nobody does it. That's why it works.  
The fakes get sniffed out. Communities are immune systems, and "founder pretending to be a happy customer" is the most recognized antigen on the internet. Meanwhile, six months of being visibly helpful makes you the name *other people* bring up when the question is asked and you're not even in the thread. That's the moment that matters, for two readers at once: the humans in the room, and the models reading it.

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: Your docs are a salesperson
content:
There's also a quieter tactic hiding in the Vercel story, and it's the most underrated marketing asset in software: **documentation.**  
Vercel didn't court ChatGPT. It had unusually good public docs and a community that discussed it constantly. The models, trained and retrieving on all of it, absorbed that gravity.  
Public, thorough, honestly written documentation is content marketing that never feels like marketing. It's fact-dense by nature. It answers real questions. Both buyers and machines treat it as ground truth.  
(You'll hear about tricks here: special files for AI crawlers, magic markup. Google's own guidance says no such thing is required, and none of it has demonstrated effects. The docs themselves are the play.)  
> 💡 **In one line:** If your product is technical at all, your docs may quietly be your best salesperson. Write them like you know it.

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: The Flood, and Why It Helps You
content:
Now address the elephant. Everyone else has AI too, and they're using it to flood the web.  
The cost of producing a thousand plausible blog posts has fallen to roughly zero. So the volume of synthetic, optimized, content-shaped material is exploding. You met this as "workslop" in Chapter 2. Founders look at the flood and despair: how do I stand out when anyone can generate infinite content?  
Flip it. The flood is the best thing that ever happened to founders with real substance.  
When content was expensive, having content at all was a differentiator. Now that content is free, **content is worthless**. The differentiator moves to what can't be generated on demand: real numbers from your own operations, real lessons from your own failures, real expertise checkable against reality.  
The Princeton finding is the mechanism. Models reward exactly the fact-density that slop, by construction, lacks. A generated post about "10 tips for e-commerce images" contains nothing a model can't already say. Your post containing actual rejection rates by marketplace is the one worth citing.  
> 💡 **In one line:** Scarcity didn't disappear. It moved up a level, from words to facts earned by doing.  
Google has been clearer here than people give it credit for. AI-generated content is not penalized for being AI-generated. What violates its spam policies is "scaled content abuse": mass-producing pages to manipulate rankings, regardless of how they were made.  
> ⚠️ **Myth:** "Google will punish you for using AI to write." No. The offense is publishing slop at scale, and the platforms are now explicitly hunting it. The tool is neutral.  
So the play is almost embarrassingly aligned with virtue. Use AI freely to draft, structure, and polish. Then make sure every page you publish contains something true that only you could have written. Fewer, denser, realer pages. The flood buries everyone who writes like the flood.  
---

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: The New Channel Nobody Has Figured Out Yet
content:
Here's the part that should excite you more than the click-decline scares you. The AI assistants are themselves becoming a serious source of customers. And almost nobody has systematized courting them, which means the field is still open.  
> **Key term: referral traffic** means visitors who arrive at your site by clicking a link somewhere else. AI assistants are now sending this traffic, and they show up in your analytics as referrers.  
Similarweb found that AI platforms drove over **1.13 billion referral visits** to websites in a single month. That's up more than **357 percent year over year**, with ChatGPT supplying about **80 percent** of it.  
And early panel data suggests those visitors convert at rates rivaling paid search. Presumably because they did their comparison shopping inside the conversation and arrived half-sold.  
(Vendor data again. Hedge accordingly. But the direction is consistent everywhere.)

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: Citation rate: the new KPI
content:
So treat AI answers as a channel and measure it like one. The metric being born is **citation rate**: when the AI assistants answer the questions your customers ask, how often do you appear?  
> **Key term: citation rate** is your share of answers. Out of the questions buyers ask the AI assistants, how often does your name come up?  
You can buy this measurement. A whole tracker industry has sprung up, its leader raising at unicorn valuations within two years of existing. That tells you the need is real and the category is frothy.  
Or you can start the way I'd start: a spreadsheet and an hour a month.  
1. Write down the **ten questions** a buyer in your category actually asks.
2. Ask them, monthly, across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity.
3. Record who gets named.  
That's your share-of-answer, and your competitors' too. Watching it move tells you whether the quotable pages and community mentions are working, for the price of lunch. Add referral tracking on your site and you have the full loop.

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: When the AI gets you wrong
content:
One scenario your spreadsheet will eventually surface: the AI mentions you and *gets you wrong.* It describes a product you sunset two years ago. It quotes pricing from an old blog post. It confidently attributes a competitor's feature to you.  
There's no help desk to call. You can't file a ticket with a language model. But the fix follows from everything above, because the model is only ever reciting the room.  
- **Audit what the web says about you.** Your own stale pages are the usual culprits, and they're the part you control by lunchtime.

You can't edit the model. You can absolutely edit the room it learned from.

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: Some Companies Are Sold, Not Found
content:
Now a correction to this whole chapter, before it convinces you that discovery is the only path to customers.  
The newest of my companies has, as of this writing, no SEO strategy, no content plan, and no citation-rate spreadsheet. On purpose.  
It's an enterprise product. Its distribution plan is older than the search engine: my co-founder owns the customer relationships, and the next hire we're discussing is a salesperson who can walk into enterprise accounts. If that plan works, no algorithm will have been involved. Search was never going to sell a company-wide operations platform to a corporation. A human being with a relationship and a demo does that, meeting by meeting.  
I'm telling you this because the discovery panic has a blind spot: *not every company is discovered.*  
- Products with **many small buyers** are found, through search, AI answers, app stores. Everything in this chapter applies with full force.
- Products with **few large buyers** are **sold**, through relationships, outbound, and salespeople. For them, this chapter is mostly garnish.  
Plenty of durable companies are built entirely on the second motion. The quiet B2B firm with twelve enterprise clients and zero web presence is a cliché because it works.  
The honest question isn't "how do I win AI search?" It's "is my customer the kind who finds, or the kind who's sold to?" Answer that first.  
And notice what the sold-not-found path *does* require: someone who owns demand. For us that's a co-founder with the relationships. Which is just Chapter 5's lesson, learned the expensive way, finally applied. We didn't start building until we knew where the customers would come from.

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: The Deeper Answer: Own Your Audience
content:
Whichever motion you run, I'd be repeating the book's worst-learned lesson if I let you walk away thinking the answer is to win the algorithm.  
Every channel in this chapter, Google's results, the AI summary, the chatbot referral, is **rented land**. It's run by a platform that can change the rules overnight, exactly as Chapter 5 warned. Optimizing for AI search is worth doing. Building your company on it is building on someone else's ground again.  
The durable answer is the one that killed RadhaRatn for not having it: *own your audience directly.* An email list. A community you run. Customers who know your name and would seek you out if every search engine on earth changed its algorithm tomorrow.  
There's no hard statistic I can hand you for this. It's reasoning, not data. But it's the reasoning the whole book has been building toward: rent the channels, optimize them, take every customer they send, and use those customers to build the one asset no platform can take back.  
> 💡 **In one line:** Get cited by the machines, and own the inbox.

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: My own confession
content:
Here I owe you the confession that makes this section honest instead of preachy. *I own nothing.*  
No email list. No community. No following. Four products and a decade of building, and if every platform changed its rules tomorrow, I could not reach a single customer directly.  
Every lesson in this section is one I'm acting on for the first time right now. This book is, among other things, the first owned-audience asset I have ever tried to build.  
I tell you that for two reasons.  
First, because you're likely in the same position. The advice "you should have started an email list five years ago" is useless to both of us. The actionable version is: **start it with customer number one of whatever you ship next.** The list you start today is five years old in five years.  
Second, because it shows how cheap the start actually is. A signup box. A promise of something worth reading. The discipline to collect a relationship at every point where someone shows interest.  
You don't need an audience-building strategy. You need to stop letting interested people leave without a way to reach them again. Everything else compounds from there.

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: The Whole Playbook, in Order
content:
This chapter has covered a lot of ground. Here is the actual to-do list, sequenced, for a found-not-sold product.  
1. **Write down the ten questions** your buyer asks on the way to a product like yours. Not your keywords. Their *questions*.
2. **Build the best answer page for each one.** Rewritten fact-dense and quotable. This is weeks of work, not months.
3. **Pick your three communities and start the ten-to-one discipline today.** Its compounding is the slowest, so start it first.
4. **Set up the measurement loop.** The monthly share-of-answer spreadsheet across the major assistants, plus AI referrers in your analytics.
5. **Put an email capture on every page that gets traffic,** and give people one honest reason to use it.  
Then hold the course for two quarters before judging any of it. Every mechanism in this chapter compounds, and none of it demos well in week one.  
> ✅ **Do this:** If you do only one thing, do step 2. One page that is truly the best answer to one real question is the seed every other tactic waters.  
---

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: Be the Answer, and Own the Asking
content:
So, the dread you started with: "if ChatGPT doesn't cite me, am I invisible?" It has a calm answer.  
No.  
You're invisible if you have no reputation the model can find, no quotable substance for it to lift, no salesperson where search doesn't reach, and no audience of your own to fall back on. None of those is fixed by a secret GEO trick. All of them are fixed by the unglamorous work this book keeps returning to.  
- Be genuinely the best answer to a real question.
- Say it in clear, quotable, fact-dense language a machine can lift with your name attached.
- Earn mentions in the places your buyers actually gather, because the models are reading the room.
- If your customers are sold rather than found, put your energy into the human who sells.
- Take the customers the new AI channels send while your competitors are still panicking.
- Turn every one of them into a relationship you own outright, so that no algorithm change is ever again an existential event.  
Search changed. It will change again. The founders who get discovered through all of it are the ones who were never really depending on a single doorway in the first place.  
---

chapter: Chapter 12: Getting Found When Search Changes
section: Getting Found in a Nutshell
content:
> 💡 **In one line:** Be the best, quotable answer to a real question, get spoken well of where your buyers gather, and turn every customer the machines send you into one you own directly.  
**The big ideas:**  
- **The shift is real but it's a split, not a death.** When Google shows an AI summary, website clicks roughly halve (15% to 8%), only ~1% click a link inside it, and ~26% just end the session. About 60% of searches already ended click-free. Gartner predicts search volume falls ~25% by 2026. Three-quarters still remains.
- **GEO is mostly SEO.** Google's own guidance: no special technical requirements for AI Overviews beyond being indexable. Don't pay for a secret method.
- **Fact-density gets you cited.** A Princeton study found citations, quotations, and especially statistics lifted AI visibility up to 40%. Keyword stuffing did nothing. Off-site brand mentions beat backlinks. Be well spoken of in the room.
- **AI is a real new channel.** Similarweb: AI platforms drove over 1.13 billion referral visits in one month, up 357% year-over-year, ChatGPT ~80% of it. Vercel's ChatGPT signups went from under 1% to ~10% in months. Track your **citation rate**.
- **Some companies are sold, not found.** If your customers are few and large, put your energy into the human who sells.
- **Every channel is rented land.** The durable fix is an audience you own: an email list, a community. Get cited by the machines and own the inbox.  
> ✅ **Do this:** Write down the ten questions your buyer actually asks, and build one genuinely best answer page for the first one. Then put an email signup on it. Start the owned-audience list with the very next customer you get.

chapter: Conclusion: The Founder's Role in an AI World
section: Opening
content:
> *AI collapsed the cost of building. It did nothing to the cost of judgment. Your whole company lives in the gap between those two.*  
We started this book with a **$115 bill** and the two facts it forced together: the technology mostly works, and the projects mostly fail. Twelve chapters later, you've seen why both stay true at once. And if a single thread runs through all of them, it's this. AI collapsed the cost of *building*. It did almost nothing to the cost of *judgment*. The whole future of your company lives in the gap between those two.  
So let me answer, at the end, the question that's really underneath this whole book, the one founders ask in their quietest moments. If the machine can write the code, design the thing, draft the copy, and do it faster every year, *what is actually left for me to do?*  
The honest answer is: almost everything that ever mattered.

chapter: Conclusion: The Founder's Role in an AI World
section: The one-person unicorn, examined honestly
content:
You've heard the dream. The solo founder who builds a hundred-million-dollar company with no employees, just them and a fleet of AIs. Let me be straight with you, because this book has tried to be straight throughout. The *building* half of that dream is now real, and I've half-lived it. I took Stemy from an abandoned idea to a deployed product in **three weeks**, alone, because AI did the work of the five engineers I didn't have. The leverage is not hype. It's the realest thing in this book.  
But the durable, money-making half of that dream has thin proof under it, and you know exactly why, because you read Chapters 3 through 12. Building was never the bottleneck that stopped you. Distribution was, and it killed RadhaRatn and Bholuma and nearly everything else I made. Defensibility was. Trust, reliability, pricing that doesn't bankrupt you, a moat the model can't hand your competitor, a way to get found, an audience that's yours.  
AI made you able to *build* a company alone. It did not make a company *succeed* alone, because the parts that decide success were never the parts AI automated. The solo-founder fantasy quietly assumes that once building is free, everything else is easy. The entire middle of this book is the proof that it's the reverse. Once building is free, everything else is *all that's left*, and all that's left is the hard part.
